Feedback is information you receive about something you did or produced, which tells you how well it worked, how it was received, or what effect it had.

Think of it as a response that travels back to the source. You do something → the world reacts → that reaction comes back to you → that return signal is feedback.
Breaking It Down with an Analogy

Imagine you throw a ball at a wall. The way it bounces back — at what angle, at what speed, whether it bounced at all — tells you something about how you threw it. That information returning to you is feedback.

You are the source. Your throw is the action. The bounce is the feedback.
The Everyday Meaning

In everyday life, feedback is most often comments, opinions, reactions, or assessments that someone gives you about your work, behavior, or performance — so you know what you are doing well and what needs to improve.

Examples:

  • A teacher reads your essay and writes comments on it. Those comments are feedback.
  • You cook a meal for a friend, and they say "this is delicious but needs more salt." That is feedback.
  • A manager tells an employee "your presentation was clear, but you spoke too fast." That is feedback.
  • A customer fills out a form rating a product and writing suggestions. That is feedback.

Notice something common in all these cases: feedback is not random. It is information specifically about something you produced or did. It refers back to a previous action.
Feedback Is Always Tied to Something Before It

This is a crucial point. Feedback does not exist in a vacuum. It is always a response to something. You cannot receive feedback about something you haven't done yet, or something nobody has experienced yet.

This is what separates feedback from general opinions or advice. Advice can come before you act. Feedback comes after.
Positive, Negative, and Constructive Feedback

People often categorize feedback by its nature:

Positive feedback tells you that something worked well, that you are on the right track, or that what you did had a good effect. It affirms and encourages. It is not just flattery — genuine positive feedback is specific and informative. "Your explanation of that topic was very clear — the example you used made it easy to follow." That tells you what you did well.

Negative feedback tells you that something didn't work, went wrong, or had an unwanted effect. It points out problems or weaknesses. "Your report had several factual errors in the second section." This tells you what needs fixing.

Constructive feedback is feedback — positive or negative — that is given in a way that is actually useful and actionable. It does not just say "this is bad." It explains what is wrong and often suggests how to improve. Constructive feedback is the most valuable kind because it gives you something to work with.

The opposite of constructive feedback is destructive feedback — harsh, vague, demoralizing criticism that tears down without helping. "This is terrible" is not useful feedback. "This is terrible" tells you nothing about what to fix or how.
Feedback Does Not Always Come from a Person

Feedback is not limited to human opinions. The world itself can give you feedback:

  • You reach out to touch a hot stove. Your hand hurts. The pain is feedback — it tells you the action was dangerous.
  • A business launches a new product. Sales are low. That data is feedback — the market is telling the company something about the product.
  • You try a new workout routine. You feel stronger after a month. Your body's response is feedback about the effectiveness of the routine.

In all these cases, something happened as a result of an action, and that result carried information back to the source.
Feedback in Systems: The Loop

This is where the word gains a deeper, more technical meaning — but even for a general learner, understanding this is important because it explains the logic behind the word.

A feedback loop is a cycle where the output (the result) of something is fed back into the system that produced it, influencing what happens next.

There are two kinds:

Negative feedback loop (in the technical sense): The result corrects or counteracts the original action. It keeps a system stable. A thermostat is the classic example. When the room gets too hot, the thermostat turns off the heater. The output (heat) feeds back into the system and reduces the cause. Your body does this constantly — when your blood sugar rises, your body releases insulin to bring it down. This self-correcting loop is called negative feedback because it works against the change to maintain balance.

Positive feedback loop: The result amplifies the original action. It pushes a system further in the same direction, making changes bigger over time. If a rumor starts spreading and causes people to panic, the panic causes more people to repeat the rumor, which causes more panic. Each round feeds the next. This is a positive feedback loop — not "good," but "adding more in the same direction."

The most familiar everyday example of positive feedback in a physical sense is the screeching sound you hear when a microphone is held too close to a speaker. The microphone picks up sound from the speaker, sends it back through the speaker, which makes it louder, which the microphone picks up again, and it amplifies in a loop until you get that piercing screech. That sound is literally called feedback.
Feedback Can Be Direct or Indirect

Direct feedback is explicit — it is clearly given as a response to your action. "Here are my thoughts on your draft."

Indirect feedback is implied through behavior or data. If you post something online and nobody engages with it, the silence itself is a form of feedback. If nobody is buying your product, that is the market giving you indirect feedback.
Feedback Can Be Immediate or Delayed

Some feedback arrives right away. You make a joke; people laugh immediately. You touch something hot; you feel pain instantly.

Some feedback is delayed. A student submits an exam and waits two weeks for grades. A company releases a product and waits months to see if it sells well.

The timing of feedback matters. Faster feedback usually makes it easier to learn and adjust, because the connection between the action and the result is clearer.
Feedback vs. Related Words

To make the meaning sharp, it helps to compare it with closely related words:

Feedback vs. Criticism: Criticism is a subset of feedback. All criticism is feedback, but not all feedback is criticism. Feedback is broader — it includes praise, data, reactions, all kinds of responses. Criticism specifically points out faults or flaws.

Feedback vs. Advice: Advice is forward-looking — it tells you what to do next. Feedback is backward-looking — it responds to what you already did. A mentor may give you feedback on your past work AND advice for your future work, but they are separate things.

Feedback vs. Evaluation/Assessment: These words refer to a judgment or rating of something. Evaluation tells you how good or bad something is, often with a score or grade. Feedback is richer — it explains why something worked or didn't, and often suggests what to do about it. An evaluation can be a form of feedback, but feedback is usually more detailed and actionable.

Feedback vs. Review: A review is a structured, often formal assessment. Feedback can be informal, quick, and conversational. Your boss may give you feedback in a hallway conversation; a review is typically scheduled and documented.
Why Feedback Matters

Feedback is essential to learning and improvement. Without feedback, you cannot know whether what you are doing is working. You are operating blind.

Consider any skill — writing, cooking, playing music, coding, managing people. Every time you get feedback, you learn something. You find out where your understanding is correct and where it has gaps. You learn what others value. You learn what your actions actually produce in the world, versus what you thought they would produce.

That gap — between what you intended and what actually happened — is exactly what feedback bridges.
Summary

To pull it all together:

Feedback (noun) is information that comes back to a source — a person, an organization, or a system — in response to an action, output, or performance. It tells the source how well something worked, what effect it had, or how it was received. It can come from people (as comments, opinions, or reactions), from data (like sales figures or error reports), or from the environment itself (like physical pain or the absence of a desired result). It can be positive (affirming what works), negative (identifying what doesn't), or constructive (specific and actionable). It is a return signal — information looping back — that makes learning, adjustment, and improvement possible.
